alt="NT and NTN architecture comparison"
style="display: block; width: 100%; max-height: 70vh; margin: 0.5rem auto 0;"

### Architecture for backhaul use case

- The NTN network is used to provide connectivity between two terrestrial networks (e.g., two base stations) that are not directly connected.
- This is transparent to end users, who are connected to the terrestrial networks that are connected through the NTN network.

<img
src="assets/architecture__backhaul.svg"
alt="NTN architecture targeted at backhaul use case"
style="display: block; width: 100%; max-height: 70vh; margin: 0.5rem auto 0;"
/>



### Definitions

- *Transparent* (bent-pipe/relay) or *regenerative* (on-board processing) payloads
- Regenerative payloads: implement on-board switching and routing (i.e. gNB tasks)⇒ less dependent on the terrestrial network, and can provide direct access to the NTN user equipment (UE). Ideal for areas with limited terrestrial coverage.
- **Gateways** have different roles: in transparent provides a bridge between the NTN and the terrestrial network, while in regenerative connects the NTN payload to 5G Core Network.


### Starlink architecture {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

![source: [@starlink2024latency]](assets/starlink__architecture.png)

## Architecture stack: overview

![source: Perplexity AI](assets/architecture__stack.png)

### Architecture stack: Layer 1 - PHY

Controls **physical layer** (PHY, ,i.e. "radio") aspects[^l1_ref]:

- Radio interface
- Channel coding and modulation schemes.
- MIMO processing and beamforming
- Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ) buffering

[^l1_ref]: See [5G NTN Stack Architecture](https://gatehousesatcom.com/product/5g-ntn-new-radio/5g-ntn-new-radio-gnodeb/){target="_blank"}

### Architecture stack: Layer 2 - MAC

Controls **Medium Access Control** (MAC, i.e. protocol) aspects of the radio interface:

- Manages scheduling and multiplexing
- Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ) management and execution:
    - Combine retransmissions to improve reliability and reduce latency.
    - Replay a packet after an error
    - Manage ACK/NACK feedback from the receiver
- For NTN, MAC includes HARQ adaptations for longer round‑trip time (RTT) delays.

## Transition: from architecture to coverage geometry

- Architecture defines processing location and control loops.
- Geometry and beams define what area can be covered and with which dynamics.
- Next, we translate these choices into coverage building blocks.

### Types of Platforms

| Platform type  | Altitude |
|:---------------|:--------:|
| Airborne (Unmanned Aerial Vehicles or UAV) | ~10 km |
| High Altitude Platform System (HAPS)       | 20 km - 50 km |
| Satellite at Low Earth Orbit (LEO)         | 300 km - 3000 km |
| Satellite at Medium Earth Orbit (MEO)      | 6000 km - 8000 km |
| Satellite at Geostationary Orbit (GEO)     | ~36000 km |

### Satellite platforms

Qualitative comparison between satellite platforms

| Characteristic |    GEO   |     MEO  |    LEO   |
|:---------------|:--------:|:--------:|:--------:|
| Orbit height |  ~36,000 km | 6,000-8,000 km | 300-3,000 km |
| Propagation delay |  ~120 ms | 23-83 ms | 1-5 ms |
| Num. sats for Earth coverage    | 3 |  ~6 | Hundreds  |
| Type of beams       | fixed | Quasi-fixed / moving | Quasi-fixed / moving |
| Num. gateways  | very few   | few | numerous |
| Target service | low-rate, delay-tolerant | medium-rate, medium-latency | high-rate, low-latency |

### Orbits

Orbital period

$$
T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{\mu}}
$$

where:

- $a$ is the semi-major axis of the orbit and
- $\mu$ is the standard gravitational parameter of the pulling body (i.e., Earth).

### Orbit examples

Some examples of gravitational parameters:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\mu_{Earth} = 3.986 \times 10^{14} m^3/s^2 \\
\mu_{Moon} = 4.904 \times 10^{12} m^3/s^2 \\
\mu_{Mars} = 4.282 \times 10^{13} m^3/s^2 \\
\end{array}
$$

$$
T_{GEO} \approx 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{(35,793 + 6,371 km)^3}{\mu_{Earth}}} \approx 86,161 s \approx 24 h \\
T_{LEO} \approx 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{(600 + 6,371 km)^3}{\mu_{Earth}}} \approx 5,792 s \approx 1.6 h
$$

### Starlink constellation {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

- [Orbital elements](https://celestrak.org/NORAD/elements/gp.php?GROUP=starlink&FORMAT=csv) in Two Line Elements (TLE) format. Allows orbit computation using the SGP4 orbital model[^sgp4_python]

```text
STARLINK-1008
1 44714U 19074B   26215.97871058  .00029734  00000+0  37585-3 0  9997
2 44714  53.1486 198.6893 0006328  18.4929 341.6313 15.59291253371649
```
        - Inclination (deg): 53.1486
        - Right ascension of ascending node (deg): 198.6893
        - Eccentricity: 0.0006328
        - Argument of perigee (deg): 18.4929
        - Mean anomaly (deg): 341.6313
        - Mean motion (rev/day): 15.59291253 and its derivatives (in the first line)

- Satellites deployed in **trains** and then spread out

[^sgp4_python]: Rhodes, Brandon. [Python SGP4 Orbit propagator](https://pypi.org/project/sgp4/)

### Starlink FoV footprint {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}


Assuming a Starlink-like LEO satellite at $550\ \text{km}$ with a $1.5^\circ$ beamwidth.

```{python}
import math

lat_bcn, lon_bcn = 41.3874, 2.1686
alt_km = 550
half_angle_beamwidth_deg = 1.5

half_angle_rad = math.radians(half_angle_beamwidth_deg)
gamma_rad = math.asin((R_E + alt_km) / R_E * math.sin(half_angle_rad)) - half_angle_rad
area_km2 = 2.0 * math.pi * (R_E**2) * (1.0 - math.cos(gamma_rad))

lat_curve, lon_curve = compute_boundary_lat_lon(
    lat_bcn,
    lon_bcn,
    alt_km,
    nadir_angle_deg=half_angle_beamwidth_deg,
    n_points=361,
)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(
    go.Scattermapbox(
        lat=lat_curve,
        lon=lon_curve,
        mode="lines",
        line=dict(width=3, color="#ff4d4f"),
        name=f"Beam edge ({half_angle_beamwidth_deg:g}º half-angle, A = {area_km2:,.0f} km²)",
    )
)
fig.add_trace(
    go.Scattermapbox(
        lat=[lat_bcn],
        lon=[lon_bcn],
        mode="markers",
        marker=dict(size=10, color="black"),
        name="Sub-satellite point (Barcelona)",
    )
)

fig.update_layout(
    template="plotly_white",
    height=520,
    margin=dict(l=8, r=8, t=50, b=8),
    title=dict(
        text=f"Starlink FoV Footprint Over Barcelona (550 km altitude, A = {area_km2:,.0f} km²)",
        x=0.5,
    ),
    legend=dict(
        x=0.01,
        y=0.99,
        xanchor="left",
        yanchor="top",
        bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.85)",
    ),
    mapbox=dict(
        style="carto-positron",
        center=dict(lat=lat_bcn, lon=lon_bcn),
        zoom=7,
    ),
)

# Avoid injecting MathJax from Plotly; Quarto already handles page-level LaTeX.
HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn", include_mathjax=False))
```



## NTN Beams

- Beams are the main mechanism to provide coverage in NTN, and are defined by the
    antenna type and configuration.
- The type of beams will ultimately determine:
    - Coverage area and footprint
    - Beam mobility and handover strategy
    - Capacity and throughput

### Starlink beams {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

- **Beam steered** by phased array antennas
- Employ circular polarizations: \acr{RHCP} and \acr{LHCP}
- Beamwidth of ~1.5° [@meinrath2025starlink_capacity]
- Each satellite has 48 beams for downlink and 16 beams for uplink [@pekhterev2021bandwidth]:

$$
n_{beams\ downlink} = 8 \frac{beams}{ant.\times pol.} \cdot 3\ ant. \cdot 2\ pol. = 48 \\
n_{beams\ uplink} = 8 \frac{beams}{ant.\times pol.} \cdot 1\ ant. \cdot 2\ pol. = 16 \\
$$

- Total bandwidth per satellite: 2 Gbps (downlink) and 500 Mbps (uplink) [@pekhterev2021bandwidth]

## Cell sizing and radio node count

Coverage and capacity sizing can be approximated with two checks:

### Cell sizing: coverage-driven beam count

- **Coverage check**

$$
N_{beams,cov} = \left\lceil \frac{A_{scenario}}{A_{beam}} \right\rceil
$$

### Cell sizing: capacity-driven beam count

- **Capacity check**

$$
N_{beams,cap} = \left\lceil \frac{D_{scenario}}{C_{beam}} \right\rceil
$$

### Cell sizing: final beam and satellite count

Final beam count is the stricter one:

$$
N_{beams} = \max(N_{beams,cov}, N_{beams,cap})
$$

Satellite count depends on usable beams per satellite:

$$
N_{sat} = \left\lceil \frac{N_{beams}}{N_{beams/sat}} \right\rceil
$$

### Cell sizing and radio node count: simple Starlink-like example

Assume:

- $A_{beam}=650\ km^2$ (from the footprint section)
- $A_{scenario}=100,000\ km^2$
- $C_{beam}=2\ Gbps / 48 \approx 41.7\ Mbps$
- $D_{scenario}=3,200\ Mbps$

Then:

- $N_{beams,cov}=\lceil 100,000/650 \rceil = 154$
- $N_{beams,cap}=\lceil 3,200/41.7 \rceil = 77$
- $N_{beams}=154$ (coverage-limited)
- $N_{sat}=\lceil 154/48 \rceil = 4$ satellites (idealized, no overlap margin)

## Transition: from geometry and beams to spectrum

- After sizing coverage/capacity blocks, we choose radio spectrum resources.
- Band selection and channelization condition both capacity and robustness.


## Spectrum

The spectrum in 5G NTN is typically divided into two frequency ranges:

- **Lower bands** (narrowband)
  - Good coverage/ubiquity
  - Limited capacity
  - Application: IoT and M2M. Not intended for high data rate applications

- **Upper bands** (wideband)
  - Limited coverage
  - High capacity
  - Application: high data rate applications, dense urban areas and hotspots

### Waveforms

- Usage of Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) waveform in 5G NR, which is robust against multipath fading and allows for flexible spectrum usage.
- Sub-carrier spacing (SCS) depend on the frequency band:
  - For FR1 (L and S bands): 15 kHz, 30 kHz, 60 kHz
  - For FR1 (Ku band) and FR2 (Ka band): 60 kHz, 120 kHz, 240 kHz
- QAM modulation schemes are used, with higher-order QAM (e.g., up to 1024-QAM in downlink ) providing higher spectral efficiency but requiring better signal quality.
- Different modulations for data transmission and control channels (L1 and L2)

## Spectral efficiency

Spectral efficiency links throughput, bandwidth, and modulation/coding choices:

$$
\eta = \frac{R_b}{B}\ [bit/s/Hz]
$$

Where higher-order modulation and higher code rates increase $\eta$, but require higher received signal quality. This is why dimensioning always couples:

- spectrum allocation ($B$),
- link budget margin ($C/N$ vs. $C/N_{ref}$), and
- achievable user/beam throughput.


### Frequency plan {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

- Downlink signal in 10.7 to 12.7 GHz (Ku band)
- 250 MHz channels
- Spot beams with 2.5° beamwidth
- To avoid interference between spot beams, different frequency channels are used for adjacent beams.
- Effective Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP) of -56.2 dBW/Hz to -52.8 dBW/Hz
- bidirectional links with user terminals at X/Ku band and with gateways at Ka band using \acr{LHCP} or \acr{RHCP}

- OFDM modulation

See [@humphreys2023signal; @blazquez2024capabilities] for more details on Starlink's radio dimensioning


## Multiple access: visual intuition

![source: Perplexity AI](assets/multiple_access.png)

## Multiple access strategies

How different users share the same radio resources:

- **OFDMA** (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access): Users are allocated different sub-carriers within the same time slot.
- **TDMA** (Time Division Multiple Access): Users are allocated the same frequency band but in different time slots.
- **SDMA** (Space Division Multiple Access): Users are separated by spatial beams.

## Transition: from resource sharing to link feasibility

- Spectrum and access explain resource allocation.
- Link budget verifies whether each allocated link is physically supportable.

## Link budget


::: {.callout-note title="Goal"}
Compute the link budget (i.e. $C/N$) and compare it to the minimum C/N value (${C/N}_{ref}$) required at the link reception to achieve a **target link performance**
:::


Link budget analysis based on [@mathworks2026nbiot_ntn_link_budget_analysis] provides a link budget example for \acr{NB-IoT} NTN, which can be adapted to other NTN scenarios.

```{python}
#| echo: false

LINK_DIRECTION = LinkDirection.UPLINK

hl_geo = lambda value: f"<span class='link_perf_GEO'>{value}</span>"
hl_leo = lambda value: f"<span class='link_perf_LEO'>{value}</span>"

elevations_deg = {
    "GEO": 12.5,
    "LEO": 30.0,
}

EIRP = compute_eirp(USER_EQUIPMENT)
total_loss_dB = PROPAGATION_LOSSES.compute_total_loss_dB()
noise_term_dB = 10 * math.log10(1.380649e-23 * LINKS["uplink"].band.bw_user_MHz * 1e6)

slant_ranges_km = {
    k: compute_slant_range(SATELLITES[k].altitude_km, elevations_deg[k])
    for k in ["GEO", "LEO"]
}
fspl_dB = {
    k: compute_free_space_path_loss(slant_ranges_km[k], LINKS["uplink"].band.center_freq_GHz)
    for k in ["GEO", "LEO"]
}
G_over_T_rx_dB_per_K = {
    k: SATELLITES[k].g_over_t_rx_dB_per_K
    for k in ["GEO", "LEO"]
}
cnr = {
    k: compute_cnr(EIRP, G_over_T_rx_dB_per_K[k], LINKS["uplink"].band.bw_user_MHz, fspl_dB[k], total_loss_dB)
    for k in ["GEO", "LEO"]
}

modulation_order = compute_modulation_order(DATA_CHANNEL.modulation)
r_eff = compute_r_eff(DATA_CHANNEL, LINK_DIRECTION)
cnr_ref = compute_cnr_ref(DATA_CHANNEL, BER_THRESHOLDS)
link_margin_dB = {k: cnr[k] - cnr_ref for k in ["GEO", "LEO"]}
```

### Link budget: a four-block check

The uplink succeeds if the received carrier-to-noise ratio stays above the threshold required by the service.

$$
\frac{C}{N} = EIRP + \frac{G}{T}_{rx} - 10\log_{10}(kB) - PL_{FS} - PL_{misc}
$$

with

$$
PL_{misc} = PL_{AD} + PL_{SL} + PL_A + PL_{POL} + PL_{SM}
$$

- $EIRP$: what the user terminal launches toward the satellite.
- $G/T$: how good the satellite receiver is.
- $10\log_{10}(kB)$: thermal noise over the channel bandwidth.
- $PL_{FS} + PL_{misc}$: geometry plus additional propagation penalties.

### Link budget: free space path loss

The \acr{FSPL} can be computed in linear form as follows:

$$
PL_{FS} = \left(\frac{4\pi d f}{c}\right)^2
$$

or in logarithmic form (dB):

$$
PL_{FS} = 20\log_{10}(d) + 20\log_{10}(f) + 20\log_{10}\left(\frac{4\pi}{c}\right)
$$

Therefore, the larger the frequency $f$ and distance $d$, the larger the $PL_{FS}$ .

### Link budget: loss terms

| Term | Definition |
|:---:|:---|
| $PL_{FS}$ | Free-space path loss from geometry (distance) and carrier frequency |
| $PL_{AD}$ | Additional implementation/system margin (RF impairments + design margin) |
| $PL_{SL}$ | Ionospheric/tropospheric scintillation loss |
| $PL_A$ | Atmospheric absorption loss |
| $PL_{POL}$ | Polarization mismatch loss |
| $PL_{SM}$ | Shadowing margin |

### NB-IoT uplink example: geometry first

Before adding receiver and noise terms, compare the geometry. The largest difference between GEO and LEO is the slant range, which directly translates into free-space path loss.

```{python}
headers = ["Geometry term", "Symbol", "GEO", "LEO"]
table = [
    ["Reference elevation", "$\\varepsilon$", hl_geo(f"{elevations_deg['GEO']:.1f} deg"), hl_leo(f"{elevations_deg['LEO']:.1f} deg")],
```

### NB-IoT uplink example: design response

- Positive margin means the link closes.
- If the margin is negative, the current configuration is not feasible: the received $C/N$ stays below the required threshold in both orbital cases.
- The design response is to change at least one of the four blocks in the budget:
    - increase **transmitted power** or antenna **gain** to raise $EIRP$;
    - improve receiver $G/T$ with a better antenna or **lower-noise front end**;
    - reduce the required threshold $C/N_{ref}$ by lowering the **data rate**, using a more **robust modulation/coding option**, or **increasing repetitions**;
    - reduce propagation penalties by operating at lower **frequency**, higher elevation, or with smaller miscellaneous losses.
- If none of these levers is available, the **service target must be relaxed** because the link cannot close reliably under the assumed conditions.


### Link budget in Starlink {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

We can instantiate the same link-budget expression for a Starlink-like user link (Ku band):

$$
\frac{C}{N} = EIRP + \frac{G}{T} - 10\log_{10}(kB) - PL_{FS} - PL_{misc}
$$

and compare against a modulation/coding-dependent threshold:

$$
\left(\frac{C}{N}\right)_{ref} = \left(\frac{E_b}{N_0}\right)_{ref} + 10\log_{10}(\eta)
$$

where $\eta$ is the spectral efficiency in bit/s/Hz.

For the detailed derivation of the threshold term, see @sec-annex_cnr_ref.

### Link budget in Starlink: Derived quantities {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

```{python}
# Derived quantities
B_hz = STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["channel_bw_MHz"] * 1e6
slant_km_starlink = compute_slant_range(STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["altitude_km"], STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["elevation_deg"])

fspl_dl_dB = compute_free_space_path_loss(slant_km_starlink, STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["downlink_freq_GHz"])
fspl_ul_dB = compute_free_space_path_loss(slant_km_starlink, STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["uplink_freq_GHz"])

noise_term_dB = 10 * math.log10(1.38e-23 * B_hz)

eirp_dl_min_dBW = STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["eirp_density_min_dBW_per_Hz"] + 10 * math.log10(B_hz)
eirp_dl_max_dBW = STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["eirp_density_max_dBW_per_Hz"] + 10 * math.log10(B_hz)

cn_dl_min_dB = (
    eirp_dl_min_dBW
    + STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["g_over_t_user_dB_per_K"]
    - noise_term_dB
    - fspl_dl_dB
    - STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["misc_losses_dB"]
)
cn_dl_max_dB = (
    eirp_dl_max_dBW
    + STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["g_over_t_user_dB_per_K"]
    - noise_term_dB
    - fspl_dl_dB
    - STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["misc_losses_dB"]
)
cn_ul_dB = (
    STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["eirp_uplink_dBW"]
    + STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["g_over_t_sat_dB_per_K"]
    - noise_term_dB
    - fspl_ul_dB
    - STARLINK_ASSUMPTIONS["misc_losses_dB"]
)

headers = ["Parameter", "Symbol", "Unit", "Value"]
table = [
    ["Slant range", "$d$", "km", f"{slant_km_starlink:.2f}"],
    ["FSPL downlink", "$PL_{FS,DL}$", "dB", f"{fspl_dl_dB:.2f}"],
    ["FSPL uplink", "$PL_{FS,UL}$", "dB", f"{fspl_ul_dB:.2f}"],
    ["Noise term", "$10\\log_{10}(kB)$", "dB", f"{noise_term_dB:.2f}"],
    ["DL total EIRP (min)", "$EIRP_{DL,min}$", "dBW", f"{eirp_dl_min_dBW:.2f}"],
    ["DL total EIRP (max)", "$EIRP_{DL,max}$", "dBW", f"{eirp_dl_max_dBW:.2f}"],
]
md_table = tabulate(table, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe", colalign=("left", "center", "center", "center"))
Markdown(f"::: {{.link-budget-table}}\n{md_table}\n:::")
```

### Link budget in Starlink: C/N margins {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

Assumptions used for the threshold side:

- Spectral efficiency is fixed per MODCOD case: $\eta=1.5$ bit/s/Hz for QPSK $r=3/4$ and $\eta=3.0$ bit/s/Hz for 16-QAM $r=3/4$.
- Thresholds are computed as $C/N_{ref}=(E_b/N_0)_{ref}+10\log_{10}(\eta)$.
- $(E_b/N_0)_{ref}$ values are engineering assumptions for this illustrative exercise.

```{python}
# C/N thresholds from modulation + coding assumptions
modcod_assumptions = [
    {"name": "QPSK r=3/4", "eta_bps_hz": 1.5, "ebn0_req_dB": 5.5},
    {"name": "16-QAM r=3/4", "eta_bps_hz": 3.0, "ebn0_req_dB": 10.5},
]

rows = []
for m in modcod_assumptions:
    cn_ref = m["ebn0_req_dB"] + 10 * math.log10(m["eta_bps_hz"])
    rows.append([
        m["name"],
        f"{m['eta_bps_hz']:.2f}",
        f"{m['ebn0_req_dB']:.2f}",
        f"{cn_ref:.2f}",
        f"{(cn_dl_min_dB - cn_ref):+.2f}",
        f"{(cn_dl_max_dB - cn_ref):+.2f}",
        f"{(cn_ul_dB - cn_ref):+.2f}",
    ])

# Also report the repository baseline threshold used in the NB-IoT example above
rows.append([
    "Repository baseline (QPSK helper)",
    f"{(modulation_order * r_eff):.2f}",
    f"{BER_THRESHOLDS[DATA_CHANNEL.modulation].EbN0_threshold_dB:.2f}",
    f"{cnr_ref:.2f}",
    f"{(cn_dl_min_dB - cnr_ref):+.2f}",
    f"{(cn_dl_max_dB - cnr_ref):+.2f}",
    f"{(cn_ul_dB - cnr_ref):+.2f}",
])

headers = ["Modulation/coding", "$\\eta$ [bit/s/Hz]", "$(E_b/N_0)_{ref}$ [dB]", "$C/N_{ref}$ [dB]", "DL margin min [dB]", "DL margin max [dB]", "UL margin [dB]"]
md_table = tabulate(rows, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe", colalign=("left", "center", "center", "center", "center", "center", "center"))
Markdown(f"::: {{.link-budget-table}}\n{md_table}\n:::")
```

## Transition: from link closure to delay performance

- A link can close in power terms and still fail latency targets.
- We now check delay constraints from propagation geometry.


## Latency limits

If we define the two-way latency as $\tau = \frac{2d}{c}$, where $c$ is the speed of light, we can compute the latency for the given slant range.

```{python}
two_way_latency_s = compute_two_way_latency_s(slant_ranges_km['GEO'])
```

## Trade-offs between coverage and densification

Increasing beam density can improve spatial reuse and peak throughput, but it also increases operational complexity and interference-management needs.

Typical design tensions:

- **Larger beams**: better wide-area coverage, fewer handovers, lower per-area capacity.
- **Smaller/more beams**: higher capacity and reuse, tighter pointing/tracking, more handovers.
- **Higher frequency/wider channels**: more capacity, typically higher path loss and stronger dependence on link conditions.
- **More satellites/gateways**: better continuity and lower path stretch, higher deployment and operations cost.

Dimensioning therefore iterates between KPI targets (coverage, capacity, latency) and practical constraints (spectrum, power, architecture, and cost).
